Section 6: rule is S4_restrictive (non-person appositive, band 7 only); logic-wrong distractor: none (the template rejects commas on restrictiveness); cue: local, the S4 exemption applies; run 39 words with the key; reasoning steps 3 (left side, right side, two slots vary). items.subtype: Restrictive appositive (not a person) followed by the verb
items.passage: For a mineral to receive an official name, researchers must find a natural sample of it and determine both its chemical composition and its crystal structure. Long studied only in laboratory experiments, the high-pressure silicate ______ its name in 2014, after mineral physicist Oliver Tschauner and mineralogist Chi Ma identified natural grains of it in a meteorite that fell in Australia in 1879.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Bridgmanite” is essential information: there are many high-pressure silicate minerals, and the name identifies which one the sentence is about. Because the name is restrictive, no commas set it off, and no punctuation belongs between the subject (“the high-pressure silicate mineral bridgmanite”) and its verb, “received.”

B.why_wrong: Setting “bridgmanite” off with commas treats the name as removable, but without it the sentence would not say which high-pressure silicate mineral received its name.

C.why_wrong: A single comma separates the noun phrase from the name that identifies it; the name is restrictive and takes no punctuation.

D.recipe: comma intrudes into a unit (subject and verb)
D.why_wrong: A comma cannot separate the subject “the high-pressure silicate mineral bridgmanite” from its verb “received.”

band7_moves: restrictive appositive that is not a person (the high-pressure silicate mineral bridgmanite), a band-7-only setting
second slot after the name (the verb follows), so options vary at two positions
a fronted participial phrase before the subject makes the appositive commas look like supplement punctuation
run of 39 words with the key in place

items.notes: Subject: earth science (paleoclimate). 60 words (models' median 56). Section 6: logic-wrong distractors present (A and C fail on meaning against the previous sentence); cue outside the 6-word window: yes, the contrast that places though in clause 1 is the previous sentence; run 34 words; reasoning steps 3. Local-window solve: the window shows record and the ice, which allows both , though; and ; though, so the previous sentence is needed. Blind solve: only B. Age kept general (more than two million years) because the 2.7-million figure was a 2017 conference report and the 2019 paper says over two million.
items.subtype: Supplementary adverb closing clause 1 (L, though; R)
items.passage: Ice recovered from Antarctica’s Allan Hills Blue Ice Area exceeds two million years in age, more than double the age of the oldest ice in any continuous core available in 2019. These samples do not constitute an unbroken climate ______ the ice, as geoscientist Yuzhen Yan and colleagues reported that year, is stratigraphically discontinuous, so it preserves only isolated snapshots of Earth’s ancient atmosphere.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence contains two main clauses: “These samples do not constitute an unbroken climate record, though” and “the ice ... atmosphere.” A semicolon joins them, and a comma sets off “though,” which belongs to the first clause: it signals that this limitation contrasts with the impressive age reported in the previous sentence. The second clause then explains the limitation.

A.why_wrong: With “though” opening the second clause, that clause becomes dependent and cannot follow a semicolon; it would also illogically present the discontinuous ice as a contrast, when it is the reason the samples do not form an unbroken record.

C.why_wrong: Here “though” introduces the second clause, illogically presenting the discontinuous ice as a contrast to the samples’ not forming an unbroken record, when it is the reason for it; “though” has to close the first clause, which qualifies the impressive age reported in the previous sentence.

D.why_wrong: Setting off “though” with commas leaves the two main clauses joined by only a comma.

band7_moves: adverb closes clause 1 and answers the previous sentence (old ice, but no unbroken record)
logic-wrong distractors (; though and , though) that fail on meaning against the previous sentence
clause 2 carries an interrupter (as ... reported in 2019) so its verb sits far from the blank
key and the comma-splice option are the same length

previous oldest air record of about 800,000 years from continuous cores

Beyond EPICA (January 2025): continuous core from Little Dome C reaching at least 1.2 million years, so the old wording (more than double any continuous core, present tense) is no longer true; the claim is now anchored to 2019, when continuous cores reached about 800,000 years
Princeton release 2019: Yuzhen Yan first author, Ph.D. in geosciences; continuous cores extend back about 800,000 years

fixes: sentence 1 was false since January 2025 (Beyond EPICA continuous core of at least 1.2 million years, so two million is no longer more than double); anchored to continuous cores available in 2019
geochemist changed to geoscientist (Princeton: Ph.D. in geosciences); reported in 2019 changed to reported that year

Option shapes match the models.

items.subtype: Colon between main clauses; the second, opening with a participial phrase, explains the first
items.passage: Methuselah, a Judean date palm cultivated at Kibbutz Ketura in southern Israel, has an extraordinary ______ recovered during archaeological excavations of Herod the Great’s palace at Masada in the 1960s, the seed from which it sprouted remained in storage for four decades before botanist Elaine Solowey germinated it in 2005.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence has two main clauses: “Methuselah ... has an extraordinary origin” and “recovered ... the seed from which it sprouted remained in storage ... in 2005.” The second clause explains what is extraordinary about the palm’s origin, so a colon correctly joins them and introduces the explanation.

A.why_wrong: The phrase after the comma first seems to describe “origin,” but “the seed ... remained in storage” is a main clause, so the comma joins two main clauses.

B.why_wrong: The two main clauses run together with no punctuation between them.

D.why_wrong: “While” signals a contrast or something happening at the same time, but the second clause explains the palm’s unusual origin.

band7_moves: clause 1 announces (has an extraordinary origin) and clause 2 explains
clause 2 opens with a 14-word participial phrase that could attach to origin, so the splice shows only at the seed
logic-wrong distractor (, while) beside the splice and fused options
run of 51 words with the key in place

sources.what: Masada excavations 1963-1965 at Herod the Great's palace found date seeds; kept four decades at Bar-Ilan University; radiocarbon dated 155 BC to 64 CE; Elaine Solowey of the Arava Institute sprouted seeds in 2005; planted at Ketura in southern Israel; first plant nicknamed Methuselah
Sarah Sallon obtained seeds from Ehud Netzer and took them to Solowey; planted January 2005; Methuselah the only one to survive

band7.why: Clause 1 announces (an extraordinary origin), clause 2 opens with a 14-word participial phrase that reads as a modifier of origin, so the splice in A and B only shows at the seed, 15 words after the blank; D is the , while relation-word distractor of 6fac7f45, wrong by meaning. No semicolon or period is offered, so no twin mark.

items.subtype: Period between sentences; the second opens with a long participial phrase
items.passage: In the early 2000s, the Chilean firm Elemental was commissioned to rehouse 93 families from an informal settlement in Iquique. The architects’ solution was unconventional—a development called Quinta ______ by architect Alejandro Aravena as “half of a good house” rather than a complete but inadequate one, each residence came with a kitchen, a bathroom, and structural walls, leaving occupants to construct the remainder themselves.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The words from “The architects’ solution” through “Quinta Monroy” form a complete sentence, and “each residence came with a kitchen ...” is another. The long phrase beginning “Conceived by architect Alejandro Aravena” describes the subject of the second sentence, “each residence,” so a period must come before it.

A.why_wrong: The phrase after the comma first seems to describe Quinta Monroy, but “each residence came with ...” is a main clause, so the comma joins two sentences.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation the phrase attaches to Quinta Monroy, and the second main clause, “each residence came with ...,” is then joined to the first by only a comma.

C.why_wrong: The dash closes the pair opened after “unconventional,” turning the phrase into a modifier of the first sentence; the main clause “each residence came with ...” is then joined to it by only a comma.

band7_moves: 17-word participial opener that could modify the last noun before the boundary (Quinta Monroy)
the splice appears only at each residence, 17 words after the blank
an open dash earlier in the sentence makes the dash option close a pair (f45ae404 setting)
key and the comma option are the same length
